- Time spent waiting for you to answer is no longer counted as implementation time. A question does not change the ticket's status, so the wait used to be billed as coding, inflating the ticket's active duration and training the delivery estimate on throughput that never happened. It is now recorded separately and shown on its own line when there is any.
- A council member that asked you something and got an answer drafts with steering the other members never saw, and is then judged by members who did not see it either. The vote is now told that a draft was steered, without being told which model wrote it, so following your instruction cannot be mistaken for disagreeing with everyone else.
- The full-screen question popup is gone. It covered the logs, the phase timeline and the artifacts you would want to read before answering.
- PROM10a, which invents answers for skipped interview questions, now receives the reasons as a separate read-only section of its prompt. They are not part of the interview artifact it is asked to reproduce, so there is no field for it to write one back into, and reasons are stripped from the artifact everywhere else: PRD drafting, PRD voting, interview coverage and every downstream prompt see the interview without them. Reasons are shortened to 500 characters where a prompt reads them, because forty skipped questions at the full storage limit is a great deal of prompt spent on notes.
- Finishing a ticket without merging now opens a confirmation carrying the optional reason, rather than ending the ticket on a single click. That dialog, the cancel dialog, and the Skip All dialog all wait for the request to succeed before closing: on failure they stay open, keep what you typed, and show what went wrong.
- The Manual QA waiver box and the skip reason box are now the same component, so both cap at the same length and behave the same way. A waiver still explains one check and a skip still explains the whole round; they are recorded separately and never merged.
- Interview answers now distinguish a person's skip from an automatic AI fill. Both were previously recorded as `ai_skip`, which is why a skip reason had nowhere to display.
- Cancelling a ticket with a malformed request is now refused. It previously fell back to defaults and cancelled anyway, which meant an oversized reason was dropped while the destructive part of the request went ahead regardless.
- Skipping the rest of the interview no longer treats a choice question you answered by picking an option as unanswered. The dialog promises to preserve what is in the batch, and it now does.
- A wire-contract test now pins the three surfaces this project does not control on its own: the API routes, the live-event names, and the `doctor --json` check names. All three are read by things outside this codebase (the interface, users' scripts, the project's own install smokes), and renaming one broke those consumers silently, because a lookup that finds nothing raises no error. The names are listed by hand rather than counted, so changing one is an edit a reviewer sees.
- The live-event names are now declared as a list the daemon broadcasts from, with their type derived from it, instead of a type alone. A contract that exists only as a type disappears at runtime and cannot be asserted on; this makes adding or renaming an event one edit in one place.
- `npm run typecheck` now covers the `tests/` directory, which ESLint already linted but the compiler never saw. It runs as a second project so the application code keeps being checked under its own settings. The three release and installer scripts those tests import are plain ESM for good reasons (`install.sh` runs one with nothing but Node), so each gained a declaration file rather than being pulled into the type-checked build.
- Eleven client tests that touch no DOM moved from the jsdom project to the plain Node one. They were paying for a browser environment, a forked worker and per-file isolation to assert on strings. Membership is by content: `ManualQAView.test.ts` moved, and the `.render.test.tsx` beside it did not.
- Added focused tests for two YAML repairs that had none, ahead of the work that will change them: the type-union scalar repair, and duplicate-key removal where the duplicate is a block scalar. Some of what they record is current behaviour rather than correct behaviour, and says so where that is the case.
- The ticket navigator's width is now remembered, per browser, instead of resetting whenever you open another ticket. Everything inside a ticket's workspace is rebuilt per ticket on purpose; the navigator's width is part of the window rather than part of the ticket, so it is the one thing that deliberately survives the switch, and it now survives a reload too. It is stored once, when you let go of the handle, rather than on every pixel of the drag, and is held to the same bounds on the way in as on the way out; a width saved on a wide monitor cannot take over half a narrow window.
- Two facts about a workflow status are now recorded on the status itself: whether it means the ticket is finished, and whether it holds the project's single execution slot. Both are marks on the phase table, deliberately separate from the board column and the phase group, because those describe where a status is shown rather than what it permits: a status grouped under Done for display reasons should not thereby decide that a ticket can be deleted. Sixteen hand-written copies of the finished answer are gone, across the delete and cancel guards, the list of actions a ticket offers, the archive query, the runtime projection, the two polling intervals, the ticket card, the two log panels, the question banner, the ticket header and the runtime-stall diagnostic's SQL filter. The twelve-status execution band is derived from the same marks instead of being listed a second time.
- The state machine's list of states is now checked against the phase table. It previously agreed with a 34-entry board-column map maintained by hand next to it; that map is gone, and a test asserts the machine has exactly one state per declared phase and no others, which is what the map was implicitly guaranteeing.
- Status labels and descriptions on the client are now built from the phase table itself, so a phase added to shared metadata cannot ship without either: there is no second list to keep in step. Text for a status that is not part of the workflow is asked for through a lookup that can answer "no such status" rather than by indexing a map that would hand back `undefined` typed as a string. The board's own copy of the column type is gone too, and a dead second column map beside it.

- Every request the interface makes now describes its own failure the same way. Nineteen separate error readers (across the data hooks, the four approval panes, the question panel, the folder picker and the ticket header) have been replaced by a single one that always reports the status code alongside whatever the server said. Mutation notices and banners consequently read `Failed to cancel ticket (HTTP 409: Ticket is locked)` where they previously read `Ticket is locked`, or in several places nothing at all. Response bodies are unchanged; only the sentence the interface builds from them moves. A `details` field carrying a field-by-field validation map is now left out rather than printed as `[object Object]`, which is what the question panel showed when an answer was rejected, and what several approval banners showed on a validation failure.
- The approval screens share their common parts instead of carrying four copies each. The editor toolbar, the approve and coverage-fix requests, and the rule deciding which attempt of a phase is on screen are each written once now. The last of those had already drifted: one screen resolved the selected attempt differently from its siblings, and only one of the four reset that choice when the phase changed.
- The model catalog has its own retry count and delay instead of borrowing the live-stream reconnect delay and the OpenCode call retry count. The values are unchanged; retuning the stream no longer silently retunes model fetching.
- Tickets are normalised once, where they arrive, rather than by each screen that reads them. The ticket list and ticket detail queries put every payload into one canonical shape, and every write back into that cache goes through the same function: so a mutation response cannot reinstate the raw server shape for the most-watched ticket. The wire shape is now written down separately from the view model, which is what the compensating casts in five components were standing in for. The list of actions a ticket can offer is a runtime list in the shared workflow table, so the client can check what the server sent against it instead of casting.
- `useWorkflowMeta` reads the shared workflow table directly. It was a query that could not reach the network (seeded from those same constants, never stale, never invalidated), so its fetcher was unreachable and its loading flag was always false. The `/api/workflow/meta` route is unchanged.
- Every `git` and `gh` invocation goes through one runner. Forty call sites had drifted into six variants: most set no timeout, so a credential prompt or an unreachable remote held the daemon thread (and with it HTTP, live events and every ticket) indefinitely; most inherited Node's 1 MiB output ceiling where the established runner used 16 MiB, so the same large diff succeeded in one phase and failed in another. The runner carries a mandatory timeout, the non-interactive git environment, the shared command log and the 16 MiB ceiling, and never throws on a non-zero exit; each caller keeps its own contract for that. Push keeps its two-minute budget and the GitHub permission probe its five seconds.
- Network-bound git and GitHub calls no longer sit on the event loop. `gh` API calls, `fetch`, `ls-remote`, `push` and the remote-branch delete run asynchronously; local plumbing stays synchronous, where a bounded wait is enough. This is what makes ticket start, merge completion, the ticket read and the project-attach probe asynchronous internally; no route, payload or status code changes.
- Git delivery now keeps NUL-delimited path records opaque, shares safe-ref and generated-file rules across callers, and bounds local reset, commit, and worktree cleanup with process-tree termination. SSH setup stays non-interactive without overwriting a caller's real configuration, malformed Git config input is skipped with a warning, and remote branch deletion is leased to the recorded expected head.
- `doctor` no longer reports the OpenCode CLI as impossible to launch when its version probe merely timed out. The check names are unchanged; the verdict for a slow probe is not.
- `looptroop logs` reads backwards from the end of the file instead of loading the whole log to print fifty lines.
- Retry and session-continuation read the same failure signals. They had their own copies and could disagree about one failure, which decided whether the session survived for the next attempt. Retry now also refuses `request too large`, `payload too large` and `model not found`, which no retry can fix.
- One serialiser for the execution setup plan, shared by the interface and the server, and one reader for a stored Manual QA summary, shared by the pull-request and integration phases.
- One definition each for `InterviewQuestionOption` and `FinalTestFileEffect`, which were declared twice, identically, on both sides of the parser/reader boundary and were free to drift apart without a compiler complaint. Both now live in `shared/` and are re-exported from their former homes, so no importer moves.
- The council's draft, vote and refine tests now call those steps directly, the way the interview, PRD and beads phases do, instead of running through an orchestrator that no phase used.
- `DBartifact` is renamed `TicketArtifact`, matching `Ticket` and `Project`. An internal TypeScript name only; no JSON field, query key or route payload changes.
- The deprecated `MutableRefObject` is replaced by `RefObject` in the approval hooks, the question list and the answer editor. React 19's `RefObject` is mutable, so assignment behaviour is unchanged.
- `dist-binary/`, the default output of `scripts/build-binary.mjs`, is now gitignored.
- `DETACHABLE_TICKET_STATUSES` is renamed `INACTIVE_TICKET_STATUSES`, since detachment is gone and its remaining readers ask whether a project still has live work.
- Eight more interface tests that touch no DOM now run in the pure-logic project instead of the jsdom one, which drops a browser environment, a forked worker and per-file isolation from each. Test names and commands are unchanged. The membership list was re-derived from file content rather than extended by hand, so a sibling that renders stays where it is.
- The `server/validation` tree (which held nothing but one test of worktree path classification) is gone, and its cases now sit with that classifier in `server/git/__tests__/worktreeChanges.test.ts`, asserting which category a path falls into rather than a boolean.
- Six of the seven modules PR-13 split out of the 2,337-line phase helpers now have unit tests naming them: the log value formatters, the tool-event renderer and stream state, the todo transition summary, the per-flow council and coverage lookups, the council round's outcome counting and quorum diagnostics, and the ticket directory context. The seventh, pipeline recovery, is covered through its only export by an existing suite.
- The shared log scroll anchor's untested halves now have tests: the scroll override a virtualized log passes in, the listener re-binding when a surface swaps its viewport node, the pin being armed and disarmed by an explicit control, frame coalescing and its cancellation on unmount, and the older-page offset restore, kept, declined, forgotten, and deferred while the fetch is still in flight.
- Installer test failures now say what happened. A killed installer reported only `expected null to be 1`, naming neither the signal that killed it nor a line of its output, which is what a CI log had to work from the three times this blocked the previous release-tooling change. Both installer harnesses now report the signal and the tail of the output.
- Every YAML repair that skips block scalar bodies is now held to it, and they all recognise a block the same way: the pattern deciding that had sixteen copies in four variants, so which repairs left a block alone depended on how its own copy was written. Twelve repairs leave a literal block's text alone; disabling that skip one repair at a time turned only three tests red, so nine of them could have rewritten the inside of a block scalar with nothing to catch it. All twelve are now pinned, each on the exact line the repair does fix, placed once inside a body and once after it.
- Two helpers that were deduplicated on their copies reading alike now have coverage that proves the surviving behaviour. The Manual QA focused diff, shared by the checklist generator and the fix-bead planner, is pinned on what it asks git for, on telling an empty diff apart from a failed one, and on truncating at the prompt budget; and which failed bead a retry resumes (the most recently touched, falling back to the highest iteration when no bead carries a usable timestamp) is pinned through the recovery that makes the choice.

### Removed
- Removed historical pull-request review ledgers, implementation notes, and the `.github/audit-dispositions` folder; maintained security and install-script policies remain in the security documentation.
- Three modules with no production importer. `server/lib/shellCommand.ts` was superseded by `commandExecutor`, which resolves the shell from the command spec rather than from the host alone; `server/council/pipeline.ts` sequenced a council round that the interview, PRD and beads phases each sequence themselves, and the council tests that ran through it now drive the same primitives directly; `server/phases/interview/types.ts` held three interfaces that only the deleted interview helpers referenced. The interview-question preview formatter went with them, its only caller having been one of those helpers.
- The unreachable tail of `PUT /api/files/:ticketId/:file`. Both valid file types return from their own handler above it, so the raw-write fallback below could never run. The route now dispatches each file type explicitly and rejects anything else, so adding a third type without writing its handler fails to compile rather than quietly saving the new file as a PRD.
- `detachProject`, which performed a full project detach and had no route, CLI or test caller. An uncallable destructive primitive reads as a supported operation. `deleteProject` is untouched.
- Roughly fifty Tailwind animation class names (`animate-in`, `animate-out`, `fade-in-*`, `zoom-in-*`, `slide-in-from-*` and friends) across dialogs, dropdowns, tooltips, toasts and the dashboard header. They come from `tailwindcss-animate`, which this project does not install, so each generated no CSS at all. Verified by rebuilding: the emitted stylesheet is byte-identical before and after. The plugin is deliberately not added, because installing it would switch all fifty on at once.
- The `duration-200` / `duration-300` classes those animations were paired with, at seven places: the shared dialog panel, the toast, and five blocks in the dashboard header. Unlike the animation names these are real utilities, and with no `transition-property` of their own they applied CSS's default of "transition everything" over 200-300ms: a duration attached to animations that were never running. Those elements now transition nothing, which is how they already appeared. The dialog one is the shared `DialogContent`, so it reaches all sixteen dialogs rather than a single panel. Every `duration-*` paired with an explicit `transition-*`, such as the header chevrons and the progress bars, is untouched.
- Around a hundred exported symbols with no reader: nine SSE payload interfaces that nothing imported while the broadcaster takes untyped payloads; `PHASE_LOG_DESCRIPTIONS`, a fourth copy of per-status description text that no screen rendered; `API_TIMEOUT_MS`, documented as the default API timeout and applied by nothing; raw-content savers for the PRD, interview and setup plan whose callers build and save in two steps; the `visiblePhase` and `fullLogOpen` props on the log provider and `ticketId` on the context tree, all passed and never read; `SSEClient.ticketId`, assigned and never read; and the `.glass-panel`, `.glass-card` and `.glow-brand` styles, which no element carried. Forty-eight further helpers and types stay where they are with the `export` dropped, since they were only ever used inside their own module.
- A second `git push` implementation, and four production entry points that only their own tests still called. `pushSquashedCandidate` pushed the squashed candidate with its own retry loop, which the pull-request phase's push replaced; `recoverFailedCodingBead` requeued a failed bead *without* resetting the worktree to that bead's start commit, which the recovery the retry route actually uses does. Neither had a caller outside a test. `isAllowedFile` and `filterAllowedFiles` were boolean wrappers over the shared worktree classifier, and `ensureRepoGitignore` and `getBeadsPath` are now private to their own modules. The tests that covered them now drive the production functions, so what they assert is what runs.
- `getStatusRingColor`, which took a status and ignored it. Its one call site now names the single colour it always returned.
- Three aliases re-exported for a question-diff type that no longer exists, the three helpers behind them, an execution-setup runtime-path list with no reader, and an execution-setup barrel re-exporting three artifact names every caller already imports from their own module.
- The OrcaCode Review workflow, `.github/workflows/orcarouter-code-review.yml`, along with the paragraph describing it in `CONTRIBUTING.md` and the policy test that pinned its configuration. It put a red check on every pull request and never once succeeded: of 132 runs since it was introduced, none completed. Two separate causes sat behind that. The configured OrcaRouter router selected no model for the review engine's tool-bearing requests and had no `default_model` to fall back on, so every call was rejected before a model saw it; once that was corrected the run still failed closed, because a few upstream calls went unanswered and the action treats any partial result as unusable. Neither fault was in this repository, and the check was never a required one, so nothing about merging changes. The `ORCAROUTER_API_KEY` secret is now unused and can be deleted separately.
- The unused `server/db/drizzle.config.ts` alias. Every database script already selects its app or project config explicitly, so keeping a third config that Drizzle Kit cannot discover from the repository root only advertised a command that no longer worked.

### Fixed
- Release artifact verification uses Bash on every runner, so Windows reads the version environment variable correctly when checking and installing the tarball and bundle.
- Update-check test fixtures use a distinct future version so new releases do not collide with the running version or fail the version-consistency check.
- Project color choices now have stable list keys on their tooltips, removing React's missing-key warning.
- Third-party notice generation now returns a normal failure status on validation errors, avoiding abrupt Node shutdown crashes on Windows.
- No-follow file reads compare device and inode with BigInt precision, so Windows file replacements cannot pass through rounded file identity values.
- Beads refinement repairs a uniquely title-matched ID collision only when one explicit mismatched modification and one `before: null` addition resolve to the affected beads, with `after: null` removals for any other winner beads missing from the refined artifact. A stale added ID can resolve through a unique title, while extra or conflicting rows still block repair. Contradictory add/remove rows for a live bead become one stable-ID modification and keep valid council inspiration instead of producing a false addition/removal pair. A declared removal without an `after` side normalizes to `after: null` while retaining valid inspiration, but still cannot authorize ID repair without an explicit null. List-valued bead content is compared structurally so separator characters cannot hide an edit.
- Relevant-files artifact budgets now discard lower-priority entries first and preserve higher-priority files when the size limit is exceeded.
- Concurrent ticket starts now share an in-flight guard across equivalent ticket reference spellings.
- Windows full-suite test jobs now have a 40-minute timeout, so slower runners do not cancel tests that are still progressing.
- Starting a ticket rejects malformed metadata before workspace initialization, while ticket reads remain available and the corrupt file is preserved. DRAFT rows remain retryable after interrupted lock writes, and rollback clears SQLite before metadata.
- Escape cancels a Kanban page-number edit without letting the blur handler commit its stale value; pagination arrows follow the visible page while the input is edited.
- Failed START dispatches clear provisional model locks and stop an actor whose persisted ticket remains in DRAFT; an actor is preserved once the ticket's stored workflow state has advanced.
- Process-control guard tests use a known live process for mismatched-token checks, avoiding intermittent Windows process-start lookup failures.
- CI selects Bun's available x64 package when verifying a new Bun version, so the update no longer fails because the package has no separate baseline variant.
- CI runs pnpm 12's locked Windows executable directly, so the global install check works while dependency lifecycle scripts stay disabled.
- CI tool setup uses normal executable discovery, probes copied native binaries before exposing them, and preserves native Windows Bun lookup. Renovate keeps CI-tool major updates separate and refreshes all lockfiles together; network, authentication, atomic-write and install-policy regressions cover the review findings.
- Stable-release arguments use positional parameters so the workflow test passes on macOS Bash 3.2 under `nounset`; the release draft job itself runs on Ubuntu.
- Container builds use npm bundled in the digest-pinned Node image, removing a separate unverified npm download while retaining the release lockfile and disabled install scripts.
- The process-tree test passes child-program inputs through arguments instead of interpolating paths into JavaScript. Security regressions verify folder-discovery authentication, credential-file proof exclusions, and literal shell metacharacters in process arguments. Reviewed false positives and accepted repository-policy limitations are recorded with their evidence.
- Kanban preset tests open menus through the keyboard so focus changes in jsdom do not dismiss them during persistence and accessibility checks.
- OpenCode v2 can use incomplete fork or transfer history only as an initial starting boundary, then requires contiguous verified events after it through the idle checks. A later idle watermark lets previously delivered and drained inbox entries be ignored; competing activity after it, an unaccounted sequence gap, or a lost stream still stops dispatch without guessing event ownership or resending.
- OpenCode v2 idle waits now use the caller's deadline, with a 60-second bound when no caller deadline is supplied.
- OpenCode v1 now reports stream failures and EOF completion consistently, keeps caller cancellation distinct from cleanup, and closes its stream iterator and timers.
- Development startup treats an unrecognized response, including HTTP 5xx, on the implicit default OpenCode port as a conflict and keeps explicit URLs strict. Managed logging uses the debug value advertised by the resolved CLI, and the supervisor cannot restart a child after stop completes.
- Catalog reloads reject active prompts and, for v2, active sessions and unanswered requests. Prompts that arrive during a reload wait under their existing workflow deadline. Profile and ticket-start routing handlers preflight the config delta, recheck under the busy guard, and leave the config untouched on rejection; busy refreshes preserve cached catalogs and already registered routes remain usable.
- Workflow stages no longer replace a model's saved variant in OpenCode prompts. V2 question fields use descriptions as prompt text and titles as headers. String fields without `options` accept text when `custom` is omitted or false; fields with `options` accept text only when `custom` is true. Pending questions survive a ticket-panel reconnect.
- Doctor reports the OpenCode URL recorded by a healthy daemon, and published-smoke health requests stay within the remaining readiness deadline.
- Managed OpenCode startup treats authentication rejection on the default port as a conflict and reports rejected credentials for explicit URLs. Blank password aliases count as unset. Standalone `dev:opencode` prints a newly generated password for manual sharing and does not print configured passwords.
- Single-choice answers treat free text as an alternative to the selected option, while multiple-choice answers can keep notes. Model price ranges collapse to one label, and cached-token prices no longer appear free.
- v2 provider catalogs separate available from connected providers, recognize reasoning variants, and preserve existing provider/agent configuration when applying routing updates.
- Same-major OpenCode maintenance selects targets published for the chosen package. Deferred upgrades remain retryable, and npm 12+ allows install scripts only for the selected package and version.
- Renovate keeps updating its pull requests after the third-party notices or Node floor workflow has committed to them. It took those commits for someone editing the branch by hand, and from then on stopped rebasing the pull request or moving it to a newer release; a floor pull request stuck that way could never merge itself. `gitIgnoredAuthors` now names the account both workflows commit as, and a test holds the two together.
- Installing from the documented commands works on the Node a package feed actually offers. `engines.node` is `>=24.18.0`, where it had been `>=24.21.0`, a release fourteen days old. Nothing chose that number: Renovate grouped `engines.node` with `.nvmrc`, `packageManager` and the Dockerfile base as one toolchain version, so every routine bump of the runtime this repository develops on also raised the requirement placed on users, to whatever Node had shipped that fortnight. `install.ps1` tells a Windows reader to run `winget install OpenJS.NodeJS.LTS`; winget offers 24.19.0, two minor releases below what the same script then demanded, so the documented path could not succeed. The code never asked for it either: the newest API in shipped code is `getAssetKeys` from `node:sea`, which is 24.8. The floor is now the newest Node release that has been out for 90 days: 24.18.0 today, while winget, the slowest feed, offers 24.19.0. Two limits sit beneath any value it can take. npm 12, which this repository requires so unapproved dependency install scripts stay blocked, needs `^24.15.0`, so nothing older can be tested, and a floor CI cannot run on is not one it can keep; npm 12 is not asked of users, who install with the npm their Node ships. And the application breaks below 24.13.1, where `rmSync` silently fails to remove a dangling symlink, so clearing an execution-setup directory left stale aliases on disk and reported success. The runtime everything is built on does not move (`.nvmrc`, the Dockerfile base and the other workflow lanes stay at 24.21.0), and a test holds that pin at or above the floor rather than equal to it.
- The install script no longer refuses a machine over its npm version. `engines.npm` is removed, and `checkRuntime` no longer compares npm at all. It had been `>=12.0.2` while no Node release has ever bundled npm 12 (the newest, 26.10.0, bundles 11.19.1), so `curl … | sh` failed on every stock install with "LoopTroop needs npm >=12.0.2; this is 11.19.0" and told the reader to upgrade npm by hand first. The comparison is removed rather than only the field, because the installer is downloaded fresh for each install and reads the floor from the release it is installing: releases whose manifests are already published would otherwise stay permanently uninstallable. LoopTroop declares no install scripts, so no npm version was ever required to install it; npm 12 remains this repository's own policy for its dependency installs, in `packageManager` and `scripts/pin-npm.mjs`, unchanged. Presence of npm is still required, since the install is `npm install -g`.
- CI exercises the floor it promises. Nothing had: the lanes named for the floor run `.nvmrc`, the advisory lanes resolved a floating `24` to the newest patch, and every job runs `scripts/pin-npm.mjs` before anything else, so an `engines` entry naming a version no Node bundles went green everywhere, because each lane had already installed it. The published install smoke was repairing the precondition it existed to test. Test lanes now run the suite on `engines.node` exactly, on all three platforms, and block rather than advise: the required Packaging status waits on them, so a failure on the promised Node stops a merge without any change to branch protection. They read the floor at run time rather than stating it, so a floor change never edits a workflow. The install smoke, which already ran on every platform, builds with the toolchain and then packs, installs and drives LoopTroop on the floor Node with the npm that Node ships (the path `curl … | sh` and `npm install -g` both take) with no npm pin in between. On Windows that took more than step order: npm's launcher runs any npm installed in the global prefix in preference to the one beside its Node, and on Windows that prefix is shared by every Node, so the npm 12 pinned for the build still won. The smoke empties the prefix and checks, before it installs anything, that the npm it is about to use is the one its Node ships. `tests/workflowPolicy.test.ts` holds those lanes to the floor and the smoke to that order, and holds every other Node version in the workflows and the container to `.nvmrc`.
- `scoop install looptroop` works again, and a channel publish can no longer point users at a URL outside this project's releases. The Scoop descriptor had been serving a placeholder since 2026-09-14 (version `9.9.9`, a URL under `github.com/owner/name`, a hash of all `c`s), which are the example values from `channel-push.ts`'s own usage text, published by a hand-run of that script against the live bucket. Every install from that channel had been failing on a 404 since. `channel-push.ts` now refuses any `--url` that is not exactly this project's bundle URL for the version being published, compared as a whole string: another asset of the correct release is refused too, and so are a query, a fragment, embedded credentials and trailing whitespace, which a comparison of a parsed URL's host and path leaves unexamined while the raw string is what gets rendered: a fragment reached a Homebrew formula as further lines of Ruby. The refusal never repeats the rejected URL, which is the argument most likely to carry a credential. It runs before any network call and before `--force` is consulted, and a malformed `--sha256` is now a refusal rather than an uncaught stack trace after the network work. Because a matching shape still cannot prove anything is behind it, the publish additionally confirms the release exists, is not a draft or a prerelease, carries the asset, and that `--sha256` equals the digest the release publishes for it, so an invented or stale hash is refused rather than shipped as a descriptor that cannot verify. A definite negative refuses; only a genuinely unreadable answer warns and continues, because this runs last against a release the workflow has already built. `--version` is also checked for shape before any network call, since a placeholder version and a URL built around the same placeholder agree with each other. `aur-push.ts` and `winget-submit.ts` take the same guard, WinGet against its Windows archive rather than the bundle, and every usage example in the three scripts is now a placeholder that cannot publish if pasted. The version comparison could never have caught this: it asks only whether a version is newer, so a placeholder `9.9.9` read as an ordinary upgrade over the released version and published without `--force`, while restoring the real descriptor afterwards read as a downgrade and was refused. The script's usage example no longer carries values that publish something wrong if pasted.
- WinGet submissions sync the fork before pushing. A branch built on upstream's `master` introduces every file upstream has added since the fork was last synced, and GitHub refuses a push that introduces a workflow file unless the credential carries the `workflow` scope, which rejected a correct submission with the fork five weeks behind. The sync happens server-side and is not fatal on its own; when it is the sync that was needed, the push message says so.
- The WinGet publish and republish jobs run on Linux, as the Scoop ones already do. Writing a Windows package manager's descriptor needs no Windows, and cloning a repository of 689,147 files on a Windows runner spent 16 minutes of the job's 30-minute budget where Linux takes under two.
- Re-submitting a version WinGet has already merged is a no-op instead of a failure. The submitter is documented as re-runnable, and a merged version was the one state a re-run could not survive: with nothing open to reconcile, it committed nothing and stopped on the empty commit.
- Republishing a Chocolatey version stops when the feed cannot be asked, instead of repacking and resubmitting. The check ran inside an `if` condition, where `set -e` does not fire, so a search that failed (an unreachable source, a proxy or TLS error) printed nothing and read as "this version is not published".
- Correcting a WinGet submission that is already open now pushes. A shallow clone tracks only the default branch, so fetching the submission branch by name created no remote-tracking ref: the check for "these manifests are already there" could not resolve it, and the push had no lease to compare and was rejected as `stale info`. The branch is fetched into its tracking ref and the push names the value this run saw.
- A release with no `WINGET_TOKEN` fails instead of warning and skipping. The skip existed so the channel could land before the credential did; now that it has landed, a documented channel silently publishing nothing is the failure the unset publish variables already demonstrated.
- Native debug history no longer hides a session's rows when its persisted owner row has missing or different model metadata.
- Ticket UI-state writes are fenced across deletion epochs so late responses cannot repopulate deleted-ticket caches or revisions.
- Historical log pages recover expired cursors, preserve loaded model and milestone sections, and publish native log tails only after their boundaries are verified.
- Log follow now witnesses completed copytruncate generations, retries the initial tail within a bound, and drops read windows that rotate before their captured generation is verified.
- The repository now exposes its documented install-channel catalog as JSON, so the website can verify consolidated installation docs against the same channel table the published-release smoke uses.
- Windows tool lookup now follows `PATHEXT` sibling order before trust checks and refuses ambiguous ownership mappings.
- Windows command-script argument checks now track quote state across arguments and reject percent expansions whose delimiters cross argument boundaries.
- Installer recovery now proves lock owners have exited, leaves unverifiable executables untouched, rejects empty PowerShell values, and points Node users to `nvm install 24`.
- Installer recovery now repairs a damaged executable only with independent daemon evidence, and release repairs retain their legacy lockfile and image-inventory paths.
- Container image repair now selects the Dockerfile layout present in the released tag, so pre-layout releases remain repairable after the source moved under `scripts/`.
- Release artefact staging now uploads a flat, manifest-checked set of files, and release attestation covers that complete staged set, so verification and publication jobs continue to consume the existing root-relative paths.
- Embedded-runtime checks read the structured `doctor --json` Node version, while published binary upgrade guidance keeps its short curl recipe in sync.
- Published documentation now records the runtime floors, Bash/zsh Yarn setup, and the current installer flag set.
- Log history refreshes loaded pages and keeps model tabs and milestones available; model selection and setup disclosures are accessible, and refused clipboard copies show a visible error.
- Repeated model-output parsing reuses bounded cached results; structured YAML recovery preserves uncertain text, honors canonical aliases, and reports repairs with accurate PRD accounting.
- Merges made on GitHub, including squash and rebase merges, now finish waiting tickets while the daemon runs, even when the UI is closed.
- Toasts and progress rings use stable identifiers; saved UI and Manual QA actions use cryptographic IDs, including over HTTP LAN connections.
- Local IPv6 addresses work consistently across backend checks, OpenCode startup, diagnostics and dev LAN reporting.
- Installers protect slow-running installs and refuse insecure download redirects; release tooling limits build inputs, credentials and install scripts.
- Release artefacts now carry the matching package lockfile, attested release and container evidence, and recorded installed package versions.
- Ticket files, cleanup and folder opening stay inside their allowed directories; unavailable workspaces no longer break the board, and reconnecting live views recover missing history.
- Workflow recovery now keeps uncertain remote stops retryable across council and cancellation races, fences planning, setup and interview saves with content hashes, and preserves PROM4/question ownership across restart and partial polls while bounding automatic bead-response continuation within each bead iteration (`0` remains unlimited for that path).
- Embedded runtimes now own their live SSE streams independently, so stopping one runtime cannot close another runtime's clients or leak failed connections, while the process-wide stream cap still applies across all runtimes.
- The `--binary` installer establishes what the running daemon is doing before it replaces the executable, and refuses when it cannot; it leaves the previous version's files alone when an upgrade rolls back, gives every download a timeout and a size limit, and can no longer be run twice in one directory by accident.
- Every user action that skips something now takes an optional reason: an interview question, all remaining questions at once, an answer marked skipped at approval, an approval with known coverage gaps, a Manual QA round, finishing without merging, and cancelling a ticket.
- The model that fills in skipped interview answers can now read why they were skipped, instead of guessing blind. No other model sees those reasons.
- A `Skips` panel in the Full Log shows the whole trail for a ticket: what was skipped, when, by which action, and what the reason said at the time.
- Finishing a ticket without merging now asks for confirmation instead of ending the ticket on one click.
- A cancelled ticket keeps its reason even when its artifacts are deleted with it.
- The installation documentation now shows how downloads change over time, with source, date range, interval, metric and chart controls.
- Consolidated docs work can now consume `node scripts/docs-install-catalog.mjs`, which prints the published-smoke install recipe table as deterministic JSON, including each channel's documented install path, coverage legs, live/planned status, pinnability, and doctor or upgrade metadata where one exists.
- A model that stops to ask you something no longer freezes the app or stalls the run. The question opens at the top of the ticket, waits five minutes by default, and then refuses itself so the run carries on. If you engage with it, the clock stops and it waits for you.
- Two new settings decide whether a model may stop a run to ask you a question, and how long that question waits. Both can be set for the whole configuration, for one project, or for one ticket.
- Waiting for you no longer costs a step its working time, and no longer counts as implementation time either. A step can take its full timeout plus however long it spent waiting on an answer, and the ticket's delivery time now separates the two.
- Any step can ask, not just the five it happened to be allowed in. The interview is excluded, because it asks its own questions, and so are the steps that only reformat text.
- Browser launching, release checks and rendered third-party text now keep externally controlled values out of command shells and executable markup.
- LoopTroop now decides which `git`, `gh`, `opencode` or `npm` it runs, instead of letting the first matching directory on your `PATH` decide. Tools installed by nvm, Homebrew, Nix, scoop, a hosted CI runner's tool cache or a project's own `node_modules` all keep working, including under `sudo`. On macOS and Linux a tool is refused when its directory, the file it really is, or any directory above them belongs to somebody other than you, root, or whoever owns the Node running LoopTroop; `LOOPTROOP_TRUSTED_EXECUTABLE_DIRS` names a directory to trust anyway. A refused tool degrades exactly as a missing one does, and `doctor` says it was refused instead of telling you to install it.
- The names your scripts read (API routes, live-event names, and the check names in `doctor --json`) are now written down in a test. None of them can be renamed without that showing up as a deliberate edit in review.
- A project that ships its own `opencode.json` keeps it in git as well as on disk. Setting a step cap used to replace that file for the whole coding run, commit LoopTroop's version onto your branch, and delete the file afterwards, taking the project's MCP servers, providers and other agents with it.
- Git mutations and delivery now preserve opaque paths, validate ref names, clean up process trees within bounded time, and require an expected remote head before deleting a branch.
- CLI cleanup and daemon control now recheck worktree state and process identity before destructive actions, while log follow preserves handoff bytes and IPv6 origins remain valid. Coding and protected hook recovery preserve edits and unknown files when ownership cannot be proven, including across a hook process crash.
- Worktree cleanup preserves replacement generations and user-owned ignored files when requested; recovery protects newer appends, quarantine retries preserve final symlinks, and daemon shutdown waits for detached Git commands.
- Free Disk Space removes eligible worktrees and reports protected worktrees without counting their files as freed space.
- Startup recovery now promotes only known, proof-backed complete artifacts. Unproved orphan YAML and whole-file JSONL, including empty files, stay unpromoted with warnings, while unresolved in-progress fallback ownership stops startup with the affected files preserved.
- Manual QA baselines, drift receipts, evidence indexes, and event history now use durable, symlink-safe writes; invalid event lines stay visible with diagnostics, and locking survives process restarts.
- Manual QA quarantine preserves a file replaced during comparison, and project-path diagnostics keep control bytes from becoming forged log records.
- Opening a different ticket now starts that ticket's workspace clean. Answers, drafts, skip reasons, open dialogs and error notices used to belong to whichever ticket you opened first, and an answer typed for one ticket could be saved onto another. What you were still typing survives the switch too, saved against the ticket you typed it for.
- Live logs stop working against themselves. Every arriving line used to make the panel ask the server for the page that line had just arrived on, so the busier a ticket got the more work each line caused. Watching a run is now quiet, streaming output follows itself down the screen instead of appearing to freeze, and the log shows what it was dropping: a cancelled ticket's history, a per-model tab's output, and each attempt of a retried phase on its own rather than merged into one.
- The interface now answers the keyboard and says what it is. Escape dismisses the dialog or dropdown you opened rather than leaving the ticket, ticket cards can be opened without a mouse, overlays name themselves and keep focus, and icon-only buttons have names. Filters reset completely, saved feedback survives the save, a failed refresh stops spinning, a failed answer edit says so, and renaming an environment variable no longer destroys another one.
- Which statuses mean a ticket is finished, and which hold a project's one execution slot, are now recorded once in the workflow table. The finished answer used to be written out by hand in sixteen other places (Delete, Cancel, the list of actions a ticket offers, the pulsing card, the five-second polling, the duration clock and the live activity strip each carried their own copy), so adding a status meant finding all of them.
- Helpers that had drifted into copies across the codebase are now written once. Terminal escape sequences are stripped the same way everywhere, so failure notes no longer keep control characters that the interface would have removed; and a ticket's council roster is locked by order, so reordering it correctly counts as a change to who implements the ticket. Failures reported by the API now read as the error's own message rather than as `Error: message`.
- Types and value lists that both halves of the app have to agree on (the install channel, the git hook policy, prompt-load warnings, bead notes, the prompt timeout kind) now have one definition each instead of one per side. A value added to any of them can no longer compile cleanly on one side and fail at runtime on the other. An execution setup plan naming a git hook policy nobody recognises now says so instead of quietly reading back as advisory validation.
- Command output is capped by bytes, not by characters. A build log full of non-ASCII text could return up to four times the advertised limit, and truncated output now always says it was truncated. The interface also stops shipping a server database module to the browser, and the build fails if one is reintroduced.
- Workflow statuses are now a type the compiler checks, not free text. A typo or an impossible status could previously reach storage and the log, and be filed under a status that does not exist. Model output that stacks transcript speaker tags is also read correctly now: `[assistant][tool] summary: ...` parses where it used to fail.
- A failed request now says what failed. Every error the interface shows carries the status code and the server's own explanation, instead of the same "Failed to …" sentence whether the daemon was down, the session had expired or the ticket was gone. Ticket ids are also encoded properly, so a ticket whose id contains a slash or a colon stops asking the server about a different ticket.
- Every ticket the interface draws is now put into one shape as it arrives, instead of each screen patching up the server's payload its own way. Manual QA fix beads finally show their origin badge and their completion time, which the dashboard had been dropping; the board and the phase timeline agree on bead progress; and an action the server offers that this version does not recognise no longer renders a button that cannot work.
- A tab left open past its session now says so. The live stream cannot report an expired session (the browser gives its error no status), so an overnight tab with nothing running reconnected forever against an API that refused every request, with nothing on screen saying the session had run out.
- Deleting a ticket, or a project, now clears everything the browser was holding for it. Six kinds of cached data survived a delete (phase attempts, Manual QA rounds, AI details, bead lists, bead diffs and per-artifact content), and a ticket id can be issued again, so the next ticket with that id started off showing the previous one's data.
- A request that fails no longer looks like a result that is empty. Bead lists, approval outlines, a phase's version history, per-bead diffs, interview, PRD, beads and setup-plan content, the artifact list and the log panels each drew "nothing here yet" for a server error, so a broken daemon read as work still in progress and nobody retried. Each of those surfaces now says the request failed, quotes the status, and offers a retry. The setup-plan screen no longer reports a failed *request* as a failed plan *generation* and offers to regenerate.
- A council round can no longer finish on a draft nobody scored. Voting used to fall back to the first council member when the scorecard was empty or every score was zero, and the refine step then rewrote a draft that did not exist. An empty reply from the winning model is no longer accepted as a finished refinement either: it is retried, and reported as empty if the retries run out.
- A bead can no longer be marked done by a report that names a different bead, and a stored bead status the scheduler does not recognise no longer stalls the whole ticket in silence.
- Repair notices on model output now describe the artifact that was accepted. A repair attempted on a rejected candidate, or one that never fed the parser at all, used to be reported against whatever eventually validated, which is what raised an intervention warning on output that needed no repair.
- Interview retry failures now retain repair warnings from the rejected batch candidate, so the diagnostic describes the response that actually failed validation.
- Interview coverage now has to mean what it says, a rewritten interview or PRD has to say what it changed, and a saved interview session is checked field by field before it is restored.
- Manual QA now reads the approved PRD one way instead of three, and the repository inspection it makes mandatory before writing repair beads has to actually be one.
- A bead edit that only changed its PRD references or its context guidance now shows up in the refinement diff instead of being dropped from it.
- A git command that cannot finish now gives up instead of taking the whole app with it. Every `git` and `gh` call has a deadline, refuses to open a credential prompt, and can handle the same large diff wherever it runs. The ones that talk to GitHub no longer block everything else while they wait.
- Both pushes to your remote now use the same credentials, and so do the fetches that create a ticket and that check the remote before delivery. On a machine whose only credential is a token in the environment (a container, typically) delivery pushed the branch fine and then stalled for two minutes on the candidate commit, asking for a password it could not request; the fetches failed outright.
- Opening a ticket can no longer break it. A slow or rate-limited GitHub during a routine page refresh used to move the ticket to Blocked; background checks now record an advisory note and retry without blocking the ticket.
- A renamed file is now delivered as a move rather than as two copies, and a bead commit that fails leaves nothing half-staged behind it.
- Checks that were quietly skipping work now do it: a coverage follow-up budget of 0% really means none, a bead dependency declared in one direction only is rejected instead of running anyway, and a plan approved on one operating system keeps its own commands instead of being rewritten for whoever opens it.
- Git hook validation refuses to run when it cannot undo what the hooks do, and puts the worktree and the staged files back even when a hook fails or the run is cancelled.
- Manual QA evidence survives two people working at once, a typed skip reason survives a reload, and a repaired or retried checklist now says so instead of looking like a clean first attempt.
- `looptroop logs` no longer garbles text. A log with any accented or non-Latin characters in it grew two replacement characters every 64 KiB.
- Cancelling a ticket now actually stops what it was waiting on. The health probes it was in the middle of carried on talking to an unreachable server for their full timeout, and a finished ticket kept its retry bookkeeping for half an hour, long enough for a restart of the same ticket to inherit it.
- Two answers submitted for the same ticket at once can no longer overwrite one another's bookkeeping, whichever way they arrive. The second is refused outright.
- A bead tracker with a damaged line now keeps every valid row, reports the affected line, and exposes runtime diagnostics so the board and workspace can warn instead of showing trustworthy completion.
- Bead plans now use one canonical contract across producers, approval, and execution. Verification commands are structured `CommandSpec` values, dependency graphs use authoritative `blocked_by` edges, and unknown metadata survives normalization.
- Bead approval now checks the arrays the coding prompt executes, rejects duplicate authoritative IDs and malformed nested Manual QA evidence, and saves return the canonical records, JSONL and content hash together.
- The approval screen keeps the exact JSONL text for in-place repair, validates source-line headers as diagnostic metadata only, and refuses approval or structured saves while rows remain damaged. Draft edits retain their immutable base hash, and stale writes return a typed conflict instead of overwriting newer content.
- Bead repair diagnostics now stay visible without weakening verification, and each structured command argument remains editable as literal text.
- Git hook validation now says when it could not put the worktree back, instead of losing the validation result to an error about the cleanup.
- A command that runs out of time is now always reported as timed out. Where the operating system would not kill the process it had started, the step waited for it forever instead.
- Packaging a ticket for delivery no longer writes over local files it was not asked to touch. A leftover file sharing a name with one the branch deleted was silently replaced.
- The Manual QA screen now tells you when the checklist you are working through had to be repaired. It was only ever shown on the artifact panel of the step that generated it.
- Code that nothing could reach is gone: three whole modules, an unreachable branch of the file-save endpoint, an uncallable project-detach primitive, roughly fifty class names that never produced any styling, and around a hundred exported helpers, types and props with no reader. No route, payload or output name changes; panels that were carrying a stray transition duration (every dialog, the toast, and five blocks in the ticket header) now animate nothing, which is what they already looked like.
- An artifact whose stored content is valid JSON of the wrong shape now falls back to showing that content. Pre-flight reports, relevant-files scans, final test results and bead lists each read fields without checking them, so a malformed one replaced the artifact with "Something went wrong rendering this content", and on the approval screens, which have no such safety net, it took the whole app to the crash screen.
- A bead artifact with one damaged entry now shows every bead that is intact, rather than nothing at all, and the approval outline and editor survive an entry that is not a bead instead of failing to draw.
- A PRD draft that the server would reject as invalid is no longer drawn as though it were a finished document. The artifact viewer had its own, looser reader, so an incomplete draft rendered as a structured PRD in one place and was refused in another; there is one reader now, and a draft it refuses falls back to plain text.
- `looptroop doctor` now tells you the truth about your Node version. It accepted anything from 24.15 while the program itself refused to start below its patch-level floor, so a machine in between passed every check LoopTroop offered and then could not run it. The minimum is now written down once and enforced the same way everywhere (by the launcher, by `doctor`, by both install scripts and by every package channel), and the message names the exact version to install rather than "24 LTS". A nightly of that version is refused too, the way npm reads the same constraint, and the instructions match the machine you are on: Homebrew on macOS, winget on Windows, your distribution's packages or nvm elsewhere.
- The address bar had two owners and they wrote over each other. Opening Configuration on a ticket and refreshing reopened the dialog and then rewrote the address underneath it, so Back had nowhere to go; a link straight to a ticket could be replaced by whichever ticket you had open last. One part of the app owns the address now, and every screen with a link (Configuration, Prompts, New Project, New Ticket and a ticket itself) behaves the same going forward as it does going back. A link to a ticket that no longer exists shows the board and says so in the address bar instead of silently opening a different ticket, the logo returns to the board and closes whatever was open on the way, and closing a dialog you opened takes you back to the page that was underneath, so one Back after that leaves the ticket instead of requiring two. A ticket deleted while you were looking at it stops being named in the address, and an address this version has no screen for (a typo, a stale bookmark, a link from a newer version, or a ticket URL with extra path leftover) shows the board rather than staying on screen as though it meant something, including when the previous session still had a ticket selected.
- An approval screen no longer discards a draft you had saved. Whether your interview answers, PRD edits, bead plan or setup-plan changes came back depended on which of two requests finished first: the screen restored its defaults the moment the document arrived, refused to look again, and the saved draft that landed a second later was dropped. Edit stays off until that restore has run, so typing in the gap cannot be overwritten by the saved draft when it arrives.
- The countdown on the current step now shows the step you are looking at. Switching between steps kept the previous one's remaining time on screen for up to a second.
- Per-command help now rejects inherited object property names as unknown commands instead of trying to print them.
- Workflow phase details now match the structured bead-command, checkpoint, and marker-recovery guarantees enforced by the runtime.
- Skip All interview finalization now rolls back its snapshot, receipts, and coverage artifacts after a post-CAS failure, so the action can be retried safely.
- Council member completion now checks only that member's session ownership, so another member's active session cannot block an otherwise confirmed stop.
- Retry now confirms and clears a retained cancellation fence for every retryable workflow phase before dispatching the phase again.
- Tokenless startup cleanup now yields for pending child-exit notifications before treating a direct handle as live, preventing a recycled PID from receiving a cleanup signal.
- Windows Git-shutdown coverage now yields after process creation before requesting tree termination, avoiding a runner scheduling race that could leave a test child unverified.
- Fixed bead approval accepting records without a status or priority, and fixed malformed bead JSON bodies surfacing as server errors instead of a stable 400 response. The client now gives canonical non-nullish empty fields precedence over legacy aliases, so an explicit clear is not resurrected during editing.
- Fixed compact nested YAML block scalars, quoted sequence keys, and reserved-indicator recovery rewriting literal or folded text. Repair warnings still describe the formatting repair while the scalar payload remains unchanged.
- Fixed bead saves caching the draft before server canonicalization. The response now carries the exact records and JSONL that were written, including derived dependency edges and preserved command metadata, with the matching content hash; explicit canonical empty values still clear their aliases.
- Fixed approval accepting executable beads without `acceptanceCriteria`, `tests` or `targetFiles`, and fixed malformed nested Manual QA evidence reaching the adapter's unguarded dereferences. Authoritative bead reads now reject duplicate IDs instead of letting scheduler updates address several rows at once.
- Fixed YAML repair rewriting literal content in compact nested-sequence and standalone block scalars, and changing valid folded `free_text` when an unrelated sibling needed repair. Repairs still change formatting only; the emitted scalar text is retained.
- Shared CI coverage for these paths uses native canonical paths and isolated integration tests.
- Bead approval and structured saves reject unknown stored statuses without rewriting them; editing waits for the loaded content hash. YAML repair preserves canonical answers beside aliases and leaves list-item block-scalar text intact. Command controls distinguish their item number from the bead number.
- Recovery tests create step-cap markers through the production helper, and startup-failure assertions distinguish schema refusals from retained process ownership.
- Daemon shutdown no longer releases its lock, closes its retry path, or escalates to a blind kill after an authenticated request that cannot confirm the owned OpenCode tree is gone. The heartbeat stays referenced during the attempt, a persisted shutdown-pending state blocks generic cleanup and CLI force escalation, failed stop promises and signal guards reset for retry, and the daemon retries with capped backoff even after its listener closes. Startup records retained ownership instead of allowing stale-lock recovery to start a second daemon.
- OpenCode supervision retains its child handle after a healthy leader exits until descendant cleanup is proven. Windows accepts a stopped tree only after `/T` taskkill completes successfully and the leader exits; a failed tree request or leader-only absence leaves the CLI ownership records retryable.
- OpenCode step-cap apply, restore, staging protection, and interrupted-start recovery now fail closed for malformed, foreign, unreadable, or mismatched authoritative markers. A local marker copy cannot erase or replace app-owned recovery evidence.
- Hook validation no longer turns an unresolved crash recovery into an ordinary advisory warning. It returns a structured refusal naming the exact retained marker and the manual remedy, preserving the safety boundary for both hook policies.
- Windows live child handles now request tree termination with `/T` even when identity lookup is unavailable; once a direct handle exits, unproved numeric PIDs remain untouched. Timed identity probes avoid the synchronous Windows lookup and minimize bounded Linux refresh sweeps.
- `clean --apply` now applies the strict non-Git ticket-skeleton and ignored-file guard again at its final destructive boundary, so a race cannot turn a protected skeleton into a deletion.
- `logs --follow` now handles copytruncate with a private pending/completed generation witness, resets once per completed generation even after regrowth, retries the initial tail within a bound, and verifies captured generation before emitting or advancing a chunk.

- CLI cleanup now preserves ignored files in both its preview and final removal check, matching Free Disk Space. LoopTroop-owned runtime files remain removable; explicit ticket and project deletion is unchanged.
- Daemon health checks require the recorded instance ID. Startup and shutdown retain their direct child handles when platform identity probes fail, and timed commands refresh verified Linux descendants during a bounded startup window.
- Log follow survives rename-and-create rotation, including rotation during an active read or the initial tail handoff. Protected hook snapshot and restore mutations use the bounded asynchronous Git runner.
- Automatic worktree cleanup keeps directories when Git registration cannot be read, both during planning and immediately before removal. NUL-delimited registration records preserve project paths containing newlines.
- Protected hook recovery rejects a marker symlink even when it points inside the application directory, keeping reads and cleanup on the marker itself.
- Fixed CLI cleanup and daemon control races. Cleanup rechecks managed worktree ownership, activity, registration, and Git state before removal; signals require a matching process start token, stale daemon state is re-read under its lock, and log follow preserves byte, partial-line, and UTF-8 decoder state across its handoff. Windows termination remains forceful, and unsupported platforms do not promise unknown descendants are gone.
- Fixed coding recovery publishing a bead as `in_progress` before its reset checkpoint existed. A failed HEAD read leaves the bead `pending` and makes no execution call. Protected Git-hook validation now persists an identity-bound marker, restores only attributable state, leaves unknown untracked additions intact, and refuses reentry when ownership is ambiguous.
- Council ownership regression tests now run in the isolated integration pool, keeping their prompt mock and real Git/database setup out of shared pure-test workers.
- A superseded cancellation retry leaves the newer run's question windows intact after awaiting the old remote stop or an in-flight question rejection; generation-bound cleanup cannot regain ownership when a later cancel is marked.
- Failed cancellation cleanup now redrives from its durable, non-expiring marker across non-terminal and restart snapshots, sends `CANCEL` only after session and question-window cleanup is confirmed, and lets a confirmed CODING Retry clear the marker before resuming. Pending beads with a recorded reset anchor are safely reset even when their status update was interrupted; interview skip receipts roll back with failed CAS or canonical writes; and council cleanup remains unresolved while ticket-scoped session ownership is unreadable, pending, unpersisted, or otherwise not durably proven stopped.
- Initial coding records the bead's reset commit before publishing `in_progress`; a failed checkpoint read or cancellation during that read leaves the bead pending and starts no model session.
- A failed OpenCode question listing no longer prunes another session's local pending rows. Skip-all interview saves now use the claimed snapshot as a compare-and-set baseline, dead process claims are reclaimable, and cancellation cleanup retries are bounded and do not keep the daemon alive. PROM4 restoration checks cancellation after remote session lookup, replacement sessions remain reachable by cleanup, and Coding Retry confirms the previous session stopped before resetting its bead.
- Council and planning recovery no longer waits on a settling promise before stopping remote work, allows an HTTP 500 with nested 404 data to masquerade as a missing session, treats message-only 404 text as confirmed, or archives a document before rechecking its baseline. Failed cancellation cleanup retries while keeping coding ownership closed across a restart through its non-expiring runtime marker; missing marker content is distinct from malformed or unreadable content, which fails closed. A late-created session is stopped before its closed callback error escapes. Interview retries recover interrupted batches and abandoned sessions; Manual QA and interview edits keep their click or batch snapshot; and a checkpoint failure leaves its bead pending so Retry can safely try again.
- Execution setup-plan saves now require the loaded content hash, keep a dirty UI draft tied to the hash it was loaded from across background refetches, serialize concurrent edits, and recheck the baseline after a runtime stop and before rewinding attempts. Approval and runtime evidence refreshes use the same compare-and-set hash, so a concurrent user edit is preserved instead of being overwritten. Approval still checks the latest fetched plan. Close receipts, question listing, PID-reuse claims, and coverage writes retain their durable ownership fences instead of silently rebasing state.
- Linked dependency directories are ignored alongside ordinary `node_modules` folders, so local worktree checks do not try to read them as source files.
- A failed workspace-setup fallback prompt now keeps both attempts in its diagnostic report after the remote stop is confirmed, allowing normal attempt evaluation and retry handling.
- Failed workspace runtime setup now exposes the existing setup-plan editor and extra-note retry, while setup-approval failures keep only their supported recovery controls.
- Async Git commands inspect repository SSH configuration without blocking the event loop. Shutdown waits for admitted requests and polling before its final command drain, and worktree removal does not fall back to recursive deletion after a Git timeout.
- Non-Git cleanup rechecks the ticket-only skeleton at removal boundaries. Worktree identity comparisons retain integer precision, staged rename/copy destinations deleted before commit no longer leave invalid pathspecs, and atomic recovery can retry a source-owned publication when its destination is absent.
- Graceful shutdown now closes each runtime's active SSE browser streams before the HTTP listener waits and rejects late stream admission, so a long-lived connection cannot hold the daemon open indefinitely or affect a sibling runtime.

- Free Disk Space continues past protected or failed worktrees, returns each skipped ticket and reason, and keeps that report visible in the dialog. Ignored environment files, dependencies, and build output remain protected. The size preview shows total worktree size, and the result counts only successfully removed worktrees.
- Worktree fallback cleanup now rechecks the target generation after Git yields, and Free Disk Space cleanup for completed or canceled tickets refuses ignored files outside LoopTroop-owned roots before either Git removal or filesystem fallback. Pre-start ticket skeletons are checked without inheriting the parent repository's ignored files, while unknown skeleton entries still fail closed. Startup recovery records whether a fallback copy is complete and blocks rather than rewinding a target that received newer appends. Manual QA preserves an existing final quarantine symlink and writes a retry copy beside it, while runtime shutdown terminates tracked detached Git and GitHub children before returning.
- Shared test fixtures now use native temporary-directory paths and the isolated Vitest bucket for real-database tests, avoiding Windows path aliases and cross-worker timeouts.
- Recovery regression checks accept Windows' canonical spelling of a temporary path while still requiring diagnostics to identify the exact preserved file.
- Manual QA compares existing quarantine copies in bounded chunks, preserving distinct retry backups without loading entire files into memory.
- Quarantine comparison now rechecks device/inode identity and metadata after reading, preserving a replacement that arrives while an existing backup is being compared.
- Recovery keeps caller-visible paths stable across macOS and Windows canonicalization, fsyncs JSONL repairs, records fallback ownership before copying, and removes stale proof sidecars only for known artifacts. Manual QA drift mutations run through bounded asynchronous Git operations and serialize overlapping decisions per workspace.
- Git diff audits preserve NUL-delimited filenames, including names with spaces and non-ASCII bytes. SSH transport keeps a repository's configured `core.sshCommand`; project trust documentation now makes clear that Git can execute this wrapper with the user's permissions, including during connection checks. WSL drive paths reject traversal outside their mounted drive.
- Contained atomic writes reject final symlinks during path resolution and every recheck, including links inserted after an earlier check. Worktree cleanup rechecks its managed parent after Git yields, and project routes report invalid paths instead of turning them into server errors.
- Windows `PATHEXT` lookup skips interpreter-only scripts while preserving supported executable and command-script order. Generated installers use the same rule.
- Legacy container repairs store an explicit missing-inventory note separately from package-version evidence. Container smoke diagnostics check the reported channel and upgrade command independently, and the audit ledger links to committed coverage.

- npm publishing and verification preserve registry lookup failures when checking the stable `latest` tag. Only a successful lookup with an empty tag is treated as absent; authentication, transport, and package-not-found failures stop the workflow.
- Release-policy fixtures read the package version from its single source, so version checks remain valid after a release bump.
- Installer daemon-port probes now treat every child exit other than a connection or refusal as unknown, so an unexpected probe failure cannot authorize executable replacement.
- Published install-catalog recipes match the commands exercised by the release smoke.
- The Windows affected-file gate now fails when it cannot compute the pull request diff instead of silently skipping its checks.
- Executable ownership checks and their generated installer copies use the same explicit numeric sentinel, clearing the remaining Sonar style warnings without changing trust policy.
- Container repair closes its lockfile-detection shell expression correctly. The Windows workflow-scope test uses a shell-local Git fixture, and installer safety tests share setup while retaining each daemon-evidence case.
- Trusted program resolution automatically trusts OpenCode's canonical binary directory (`~/.opencode/bin`) and paths specified via `OPENCODE_INSTALL_DIR` or `OPENCODE_DIR`. When OpenCode is installed or updated on Linux as root, official release archives unpacked with GNU `tar` preserve the build runner's UID (`1001`), which previously caused LoopTroop's ancestor ownership security check to refuse the binary on startup.
- Phase and Full Log tabs use complete model metadata for their history scope, including models found only on older pages. Unavailable selections reset both the displayed tab and its history/export query; cached filters and reopened views cannot replace newer model metadata. Scope changes reset selection immediately, failed loads clear unavailable filters, and changing the copy target cancels an unfinished export. Export failures also clear a previous success indicator.
- Refreshing phase, Full Log, or bead history after loading older pages starts with the newest page, updating totals and model metadata, then follows fresh cursors through the loaded page count or until history ends. It no longer loses the newest page by restarting from an old cursor. New log entries can shift page boundaries, so the exact oldest visible row may change after refresh.
- Copy buttons for ticket details, paths, artifacts, individual log rows, bead logs, crash details, and sign-in instructions show `Copy failed` when clipboard access is refused. The message remains until a retry succeeds or the copy target changes, and each failed retry is announced again. Log-row status updates preserve the message, and retry buttons stay visible after failure. Empty log exports leave the clipboard unchanged without reporting a new failure; known-empty views disable Copy. Execution-setup step disclosures expose their expanded state to assistive technology.
- The model picker exposes a combobox with grouped model options. Provider-collapse controls sit above the results; arrow keys move through available models, Enter selects, and Escape returns focus to the picker button. Tab moves among search and controls; contextual labels identify each main/council picker and its current choice. Sticky provider headings no longer cover keyboard-active options, and empty search results are announced.
- AI and model history queries include model-attributed system milestones alongside AI detail rows, with matching pagination, totals, and exports. AI-only records survive an interrupted normal-file append; mirrored copies are deduplicated before timestamp-ordered pagination, while normal/system views keep file order. Shared classification preserves model output containing diagnostic tags, and ingestion derives indexed model identity and AI membership to avoid repeated JSON scans. The live log context preserves the same rows when loading AI history. Missing audience and kind fields are inferred consistently before indexing and reading, keeping plain model output in ALL counts, pages, and exports and preserving session activity detection after reload.
